question: What is osteomyelitis?

options.A: A malignant tumor originating in bone tissue
options.B: An infection of the bone and its marrow
options.C: A sudden loss of bone density due to calcium deficiency
options.D: A degenerative wearing away of joint cartilage

explanation: Osteomyelitis refers to an infection involving the bone and bone marrow, commonly caused by bacteria. [learn more](BMP216_U3_T4#BMP216_U3_T4_h1)

question: A patient arrives at the ward with an infected leg wound after visiting a traditional bonesetter following a motorcycle crash. What major risk does this local intervention pose?

options.A: Immediate development of secondary bone malignancy
options.B: Rapid healing of the fracture causing bone overgrowth
options.C: Permanent hardening of the joint cartilage
options.D: Introduction of direct bacterial contaminants leading to bone infection

explanation: Unsterile manipulation and splinting can introduce bacteria directly into open wounds or exposed bone, triggering osteomyelitis. [learn more](BMP216_U3_T4#BMP216_U3_T4_h1)

question: What is the most common bacterial organism responsible for osteomyelitis?
explanation: Staphylococcus aureus is the leading pathogen found in both acute and chronic cases of bone infection across all age groups. [learn more](BMP216_U3_T4#BMP216_U3_T4_h2)

question: Why does infection inside a bone quickly lead to tissue death?

options.A: Rising pressure from pus cuts off the local blood supply
options.B: Bacteria secrete specific acids that melt the bone matrix
options.C: The body intentionally stops all circulation to prevent spread
options.D: Bone cells dissolve immediately upon contact with white blood cells

explanation: Because bone is a rigid structure, accumulating pus creates high pressure that compresses tiny blood vessels, cutting off blood flow and causing tissue death. [learn more](BMP216_U3_T4#BMP216_U3_T4_h2)

question: Which clinical feature is most characteristic of chronic osteomyelitis compared to acute osteomyelitis?

options.A: Rapid and permanent healing with oral antibiotics alone
options.B: Abrupt onset of high fever and severe local swelling
options.C: Presence of draining sinus tracts and dead bone fragments
options.D: Complete absence of pain during physical examination

explanation: Chronic osteomyelitis is marked by dead bone segments and skin openings that intermittently drain pus over long periods. [learn more](BMP216_U3_T4#BMP216_U3_T4_h3)

question: Which age group is most frequently affected by acute hematogenous osteomyelitis?

options.B: Elderly individuals living in urban areas

explanation: Acute hematogenous osteomyelitis frequently targets the active growth areas of long bones in growing children. [learn more](BMP216_U3_T4#BMP216_U3_T4_h3)

question: How is the local pain in osteomyelitis typically described by patients?

options.B: Mild, intermittent, and relieved by touch
options.C: Burning and widespread across the whole body

explanation: The rising pressure inside the rigid bone cavity causes a characteristic deep, throbbing pain that stays constant. [learn more](BMP216_U3_T4#BMP216_U3_T4_h4)

question: A patient with a chronic leg ulcer develops a new draining wound on the shin that emits pus. What condition should the nurse suspect?

options.A: Chronic osteomyelitis with a sinus tract

explanation: A persistent draining wound that connects to the bone is a hallmark sign of a chronic bone infection. [learn more](BMP216_U3_T4#BMP216_U3_T4_h4)

question: Why might a plain X-ray appear completely normal during the very first week of acute osteomyelitis?

options.A: X-rays only show soft tissues and cannot visualize any bone structures
options.B: Significant bone destruction takes time to become visible on standard film
options.C: Radiologists cannot read X-rays of infected limbs accurately
options.D: Early bacterial infections do not affect bone density at all

explanation: Standard X-rays require a noticeable amount of bone matrix loss before structural damage shows up on the image. [learn more](BMP216_U3_T4#BMP216_U3_T4_h5)

question: Which laboratory markers are most commonly monitored to assess inflammation and treatment response in osteomyelitis?
explanation: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and C-reactive protein (CRP) are blood markers of inflammation that rise during active bone infection and fall as treatment works. [learn more](BMP216_U3_T4#BMP216_U3_T4_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of surgical debridement in chronic osteomyelitis?

options.A: To permanently fuse the adjacent joint to stop all movement
options.B: To increase blood pressure throughout the affected extremity
options.C: To replace the entire limb with a synthetic bone structure
options.D: To remove dead bone and infected tissue where antibiotics cannot reach

explanation: Dead bone lacks a blood supply, meaning antibiotics cannot penetrate it. Surgical removal is necessary to clear the infection. [learn more](BMP216_U3_T4#BMP216_U3_T4_h6)

question: Why is initial antibiotic therapy for osteomyelitis typically given intravenously rather than orally?

options.A: To prevent the patient from experiencing any gastrointestinal upset
options.B: Because oral antibiotics are completely illegal in surgical wards
options.C: To achieve high and rapid bactericidal drug concentrations in the bone tissue
options.D: To ensure the patient stays asleep throughout the entire treatment course

explanation: Giving antibiotics directly into the bloodstream ensures high drug levels are delivered to poorly vascularized infected bone areas. [learn more](BMP216_U3_T4#BMP216_U3_T4_h6)

question: What is a critical nursing priority when caring for a patient receiving long-term antibiotic therapy for osteomyelitis?

options.A: Changing the intravenous line only once every two weeks
options.B: Restricting fluid intake to prevent swelling in the affected limb
options.C: Encouraging heavy weight-bearing exercise immediately to build muscle
options.D: Monitoring for adverse drug reactions and ensuring therapy completion

explanation: Long courses of antibiotics carry risks for side effects, and stopping treatment early often leads to the infection returning. [learn more](BMP216_U3_T4#BMP216_U3_T4_h7)

question: A patient scheduled for a painful dressing change on an infected tibial wound expresses severe anxiety. What is the most appropriate initial nursing action?

options.A: Administer prescribed pain medication well before the procedure begins
options.B: Perform the dressing change quickly without warning the patient
options.C: Tell the patient that the pain is minor and should be ignored
options.D: Cancel the dressing change entirely until tomorrow morning

explanation: Giving pain medication ahead of time ensures peak relief during the procedure, reducing patient distress. [learn more](BMP216_U3_T4#BMP216_U3_T4_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a recognized complication of poorly treated osteomyelitis?
explanation: Osteomyelitis weakens bone through tissue destruction, leading to instability and fractures rather than strengthening it. [learn more](BMP216_U3_T4#BMP216_U3_T4_h8)

question: Why is public health education regarding open fractures and traditional bone-setters crucial in Nigeria?

options.A: To eliminate the need for any surgical intervention in the country
options.B: To ensure traditional bonesetters receive government medical licenses
options.C: To reduce the financial cost of importing hospital equipment
options.D: To reduce delays in medical care and prevent severe bone infections

explanation: Community education helps people recognize the risks of unsterile manipulation and encourages prompt hospital care for trauma. [learn more](BMP216_U3_T4#BMP216_U3_T4_h8)
